contenido: 1. Immortal work of the merciful God, the Church, although by itself and by virtue of its own nature has as its end the salvation and eternal happiness of souls, nevertheless seeks so many and such notable goods, even in the same sphere of temporal things, that neither in number nor in quality could it provide greater if the first and main object of its institution were to ensure the happiness of the present life. Wherever the Church has penetrated, it has immediately changed the state of things. It has informed customs with hitherto unknown virtues and has implanted a new civilization in civil society. The peoples who received this civilization surpassed the others for their balance, for their equity and for the glories of their history. However, a very old and repeated slanderous accusation affirms that the Church is the enemy of the State and that its capacity to promote the well-being and glory that every well-constituted society licitly and naturally desires is null. From the beginning of the Church, Christians were persecuted with very similar slanders. Target of hatred and malevolence, Christians were considered enemies of the Empire. At that time the common people used to attribute to Christianity the blame for all the calamities that afflicted the republic, failing to see that it was God, avenger of crimes, who justly punished sinners.

2. It is not difficult to determine the character and form that political society will have when Christian philosophy governs the State. Man is ordered by Nature to live in a political community. Man cannot obtain in solitude everything that the necessity and usefulness of bodily life demand, nor what leads to the perfection of his spirit. For this reason the providence of God has ordained that man is born inclined to union and association with his fellow men, both domestic and civil, which alone can provide him with perfect sufficiency for life.

3. Constituted on these principles, it is evident that the State has the duty to fulfill, through public worship, the numerous and important obligations that unite it with God. Natural reason, which commands each man to worship God piously and holyly, because we depend on Him, and because, having left Him, we must return to Him, imposes the same obligation on civil society. Men are no less subject to the power of God when they live together in society than when they live in isolation. Society, for its part, is no less obliged than individuals to give thanks to God, to whom it owes its existence, its conservation and the innumerable abundance of its goods. For this reason, just as it is not permissible for anyone to neglect one's duties towards God, the greatest of which is to embrace religion with one's heart and actions, not the one that each one prefers, but that which God commands and establishes by certain and irrevocable arguments as unique and true, in the same way States cannot act, without incurring sin, as if God did not exist, nor reject religion as something strange or useless, nor can they, finally, indifferently choose one religion among so many. Quite the opposite. The State has the strict obligation to admit divine worship in the way in which God himself has wanted him to be venerated. It is, therefore, a serious obligation of the authorities to honor the holy name of God. Among their main obligations they must place the obligation to favor religion, defend it effectively, put it under the protection of the laws, and not legislate anything that is contrary to its safety. Obligation owed by rulers also to their citizens. Because all men have been born and have been raised to achieve an ultimate and supreme end, to which we must refer all our purposes, and which is placed in heaven, beyond the fragile brevity of this life. If, then, the perfect and total happiness of men depends on this supreme good, the consequence is clear: the achievement of this good matters so much to each of the citizens that there is and cannot be any other matter more important. Therefore, it is necessary that the State, established for the good of all, in ensuring public prosperity, proceed in such a way that, far from creating obstacles, it gives all possible facilities to citizens to achieve that supreme and unchangeable good that they naturally desire. The first and principal of all of them consists of ensuring an inviolable and holy observance of religion, whose duties unite man with God.

4. Every man of sincere and prudent judgment easily sees what the true religion is. A multitude of effective arguments, such as the real fulfillment of the prophecies, the great number of miracles, the rapid spread of faith, even in the midst of enemy powers and insurmountable difficulties, the testimony of the martyrs and many others like them, demonstrate that the only true religion is that which Jesus Christ in person instituted and entrusted to his Church to preserve and propagate throughout time.

5. The only begotten Son of God has established a society on earth called the Church. To this he transmitted, to continue it throughout history, the exalted divine mission, which he in person had received from his Father. «As my Father has sent me, so I send you»[5]. «I will be with you always until the consummation of the world»[6]. And just as Jesus Christ came to earth so that men may have life, and have it abundantly[7], in the same way the goal that the Church proposes is the eternal salvation of souls. And thus, by its very nature, the Church extends to the entire universality of the human race, without being circumscribed by any limit of time or place. Preach the Gospel to every creature[8].

6. God has distributed, therefore, the government of the human race between two powers: ecclesiastical power and civil power. Ecclesiastical power, placed at the head of divine interests. The civil power, in charge of human interests. Both powers are sovereign in their kind. Each one is circumscribed within certain limits, defined by its own nature and by its proximate end. From which a determined sphere results, within which each power exercises its activity iure proprio. But since the passive subject of both sovereign powers is one and the same, and since, on the other hand, it may happen that the same matter belongs, although under different aspects, to the competence and jurisdiction of both powers, it is necessary that God, origin of both powers, has established in his providence a right order of composition between the respective activities of one and the other power. "The [authorities] that exist have been ordained by God"[17]. If this were not the case, frequent reasons for regrettable conflicts would arise, and many times man would remain in doubt, like a traveler at a crossroads, not knowing which path to choose, when he finds himself requested by the contrary commands of two authorities, neither of which he can, without sin, fail to obey. This situation is totally contrary to the wisdom and goodness of God, who even in the physical world, of such evident inferiority, has balanced the forces and natural causes among themselves with such concerted moderation and wonderful harmony, that neither prevent the others nor do they stop all from concurring with exact adequacy to the total end towards which the universe tends.

7. What we have summarily outlined is the Christian conception of the State. Conception not developed recklessly and on a whim, but constituted on the supreme and most exact principles, confirmed by natural reason itself.

8. The constitution of the State that we have just explained does not undermine or discredit the true dignity of the rulers. And it is so far from diminishing the rights of authority, that on the contrary, it enlarges and consolidates them.

9. There was a time when the philosophy of the Gospel governed the States. At that time, the self-efficacy of Christian wisdom and its divine virtue had penetrated the laws, the institutions, and the morality of the people, infiltrating all classes and relationships of society. The religion founded by Jesus Christ was firmly placed in the degree of honor due to it and flourished everywhere thanks to the benevolent adherence of the rulers and the legitimate guardianship of the magistrates. The priesthood and the empire lived together in mutual concord and friendly consortium of wills. Organized in this way, the State produced goods beyond all hope. The memory of these benefits still exists and will remain in force in countless historical monuments that no corrupting skill of the adversaries will be able to distort or obscure. If Christian Europe tamed the barbarian nations and made them pass from fierceness to meekness and from superstition to truth; if it victoriously rejected the Muslim invasions; if it has preserved the scepter of civilization and has remained as a teacher and guide of the world in the discovery and teaching of everything that could benefit human culture; if it has provided the people with the good of true freedom in its most varied forms; If with a wise providence it has created such numerous and heroic institutions to alleviate the misfortunes of men, there is no doubt: Europe owes for all this an enormous debt of gratitude to religion, in which it always found an inspirer of its great enterprises and an effective helper in its achievements. We would also have preserved all of these same assets today if the concord between both powers had been preserved. We could even reasonably expect greater benefits if the civil power had obeyed with greater fidelity and perseverance the authority, the magisterium and the councils of the Church. The words that Yves of Chartres wrote to Pope Paschal II deserve to be considered as the formulation of an essential law: «When the empire and the priesthood live in full harmony, the world is well governed and the Church flourishes and bears fruit. But when discord arises between them, not only do the small shoots fail to grow, but even the great institutions themselves perish miserably.

10. However, the pernicious and deplorable desire for novelty promoted in the 16th century, after first disturbing the Christian religion, came to upset philosophy as an inevitable consequence, and from this it went on to alter all orders of civil society. To this source we must trace the origin of the modern principles of unbridled freedom, invented in the great revolution of the last century and proposed as the basis and foundation of a new law, unknown until then and contrary in many of its theses not only to Christian law, but even to natural law.

11. It is easy to see the deplorable situation to which the Church is reduced if the State relies on these foundations, so praised today. Because when practical politics conform to these doctrines, the Church in the State is given a place equal to, or perhaps inferior to, that of other societies different from it. Ecclesiastical laws are not taken into account at all, and the Church, which by express command of Jesus Christ must teach all people, is removed from any intervention in the public education of citizens. In the same matters that are of mixed competence, the State authorities themselves establish arbitrary legislation and arrogantly disregard the sacred legislation of the Church in this matter. And so, they place Christian marriage under their jurisdiction, even legislating about the marital bond, its unity and stability; They deprive the clergy of their property, denying the Church the right to property; They treat, finally, the Church as if the Church did not have the nature and rights of a perfect society and as if it were merely an association similar to other associations recognized by the State. For this reason, they affirm that, if the Church has any right or legitimate power to act, it owes it to the favor and concessions of the State authorities. If in a State the civil legislation leaves the Church a sphere of legal autonomy and there is some concordat between both powers, they are quick to proclaim that it is necessary to separate the affairs of the Church from the affairs of the State, and this with the attempt to be able to act with impunity against the agreed pact, and, thus eliminating all obstacles, leaving the civil authorities as absolute arbiters of everything. But since the Church cannot tolerate these pretensions, because this would be equivalent to the abandonment of the most holy and most serious duties, and, on the other hand, the Church demands that the concordat be fulfilled with complete fidelity, conflicts frequently arise between the sacred power and the civil power, the final result of which is usually that the weaker part in human forces succumbs to the stronger part.

12. Thus, in the political situation that many currently advocate, there is a tendency in ideas and action to completely exclude the Church from society or to have it subject and chained to the State. Most of the measures taken by governments are directed towards this end. Legislation, the public administration of the State, the secular education of youth, the dispossession and suppression of religious Orders, the destruction of the temporal power of the Roman Pontiffs, have no other purpose than to break the strength of Christian institutions, stifle the freedom of the Catholic Church and suppress all its rights.

13. Natural reason alone demonstrates the serious error of these theories about the constitution of the State. Nature teaches that all authority, whatever it may be, comes from God as a supreme and august source. The sovereignty of the people, which, according to them, resides by natural right in the multitude totally independent of God, although it presents great advantages to flatter and inflame innumerable passions, lacks any solid foundation and substantive effectiveness to guarantee public safety and maintain order in society. Because with these theories things have reached such a point that many admit the legitimacy of the right to rebellion as a norm of political life. Today the opinion prevails that, since the rulers are mere delegates, in charge of executing the will of the people, it is necessary that everything changes in accordance with the will of the people, from which it follows that the State is never free from the fear of revolutions.

14. In religious matters, thinking that forms of worship, different and even contrary, are all the same, is equivalent to confessing that you do not want to approve or practice any of them. This attitude, if nominally different from atheism, is actually identified with it. Those who believe in the existence of God, if they want to be consistent with themselves and not fall into absurdity, must necessarily understand that the usual forms of divine worship, whose difference, disparity and contradiction even in things of utmost importance are so great, cannot all be equally acceptable nor equally good or pleasing to God.

15. Similarly, freedom of thought and expression, lacking all limits, is not in itself a good that human society can rightly congratulate; On the contrary, it is the source and origin of many evils. Freedom, as a faculty that perfects man, must be applied exclusively to truth and good. Now: the essence of truth and good cannot change at the whim of man, but is always the same and is no less immutable than the very nature of things. If the intelligence adheres to false opinions, if the will chooses evil and embraces it, neither the intelligence nor the will reach their perfection; On the contrary, they abdicate their natural dignity and become corrupted. Consequently, it is not licit to publish and expose to the sight of men what is contrary to virtue and truth, and it is much less licit to favor and protect these publications and exhibitions with the protection of the laws. There is only one way to reach heaven, to which we all tend: the virtuous life. Therefore, any State that allows freedom of thought and action that, with its excesses, can lead the intelligences of truth and the souls of virtue astray with impunity, departs from the norm taught by nature.

16. These doctrines, contrary to reason and of such importance for the public good of the State, did not fail to be condemned by the Roman Pontiffs, our predecessors, who lived convinced of the obligations imposed on them by the apostolic office. Thus, Gregory XVI, in the encyclical Mirari vos, of August 15, 1832, condemned with great doctrinal authority the principles that were already being disseminated at that time, that is, religious indifferentism, absolute freedom of religion and conscience, freedom of the press and the legitimacy of the right of rebellion. In relation to the separation between Church and State, the aforementioned Pontiff said: «We could not predict happy results for the Church and the State of the wishes of those who insist that the Church be separated from the State, breaking the mutual concord of the empire and the priesthood. Everyone knows very well that this concord, which has always been so beneficial to religious and civil interests, is greatly feared by the proponents of shameless freedom."[23] In a similar way, Pius IX, taking advantage of the opportunities that presented themselves, condemned many of the false opinions that had begun to be in vogue, later collecting them in a catalogue, so that Catholics would know what to expect, without danger of making mistakes, in the midst of such a great avenue of errors[24].

17. From these pontifical declarations, what must be kept in mind, above all, is that the origin of civil power must be placed in God, not in the multitude; that the right of rebellion is contrary to reason; that it is not lawful for individuals, nor for States, to dispense with their religious duties or to measure all contrary cults with the same level; that immoderate freedom of thought and expression should not be considered at all as a right of citizens, nor as a claim deserving of favor and protection. It must also be admitted that the Church, no less than the State, is a society complete in its kind and legally perfect; and that, consequently, those who have the supreme power of the State should not seek to subject the Church to their service or obedience, or to reduce the freedom of action of the Church in its proper sphere, or to take away any of the rights that Jesus Christ has conferred on it. However, in matters of mixed law, it is fully in accordance with nature and the designs of God, not the separation, much less the conflict between both powers, but rather concord, and this in accordance with the proximate purposes that have given rise to both societies.

18. These are the principles that the Catholic Church establishes regarding the constitution and government of States. With these principles, if one wants to judge correctly, none of the different forms of government are condemned by themselves, since they contain nothing contrary to Catholic doctrine, and all of them, carried out with prudence and justice, can guarantee public prosperity to the State. Furthermore: it is not even reprehensible in itself, according to these principles, that the people have a greater or lesser participation in the government, participation that, on certain occasions and within a specific legislation, may not only be beneficial, but even obligatory for citizens. There is also no just reason to accuse the Church of being too narrow in terms of tolerance or of being an enemy of authentic and legitimate freedom. Because, although the Church judges it illegal for the various kinds of divine worship to enjoy the same right as true religion, it does not, however, condemn those rulers who, in order to achieve an important good or to avoid a serious evil, patiently tolerate in practice the existence of such cults in the State. It is, on the other hand, the custom of the Church to watch very carefully so that no one is forced to embrace the Catholic faith against his will, because, as Saint Augustine rightly observes, "man can only believe of good will"[25].

19. For the same reason, the Church cannot approve a freedom that leads to contempt for the most holy laws of God and the denial of the obedience due to legitimate authority. This freedom, more than freedom, is license. And Saint Augustine rightly calls it freedom from perdition[26] and the apostle Saint Peter calls it the veil of malice[27]. Furthermore: this freedom, being contrary to reason, constitutes true slavery, since he who commits sin is a slave to sin[28]. On the contrary, authentic and desirable freedom is that which in the sphere of private life does not allow the subjection of man to the abominable tyranny of errors and bad passions and which in the field of public life governs citizens wisely, promotes progress and the comforts of life and defends the administration of the State from all foreign arbitrariness. The Church is the first to approve this just and worthy freedom of man. He has never stopped fighting to keep it intact and whole in the towns. The historical monuments of previous ages demonstrate that the Catholic Church has always been the initiator, or the promoter, or the protector of all the institutions that can contribute to the common well-being in the State. Such are the effective institutions created to limit the tyranny of princes who govern the people badly; those that prevent the supreme power of the State from improperly invading the municipal or family sphere, and those aimed at guaranteeing the dignity and life of people and the legal equality of citizens.

20. But these principles, so correct and reasonable, are not accepted today, when States not only refuse to adapt to the norms of Christian philosophy, but also seem to seek to move further away from it every day. However, since the truth clearly stated tends to spread easily by itself and penetrate little by little into the understandings of men, therefore We, bound in conscience by the sacred apostolic office that we exercise towards all peoples, declare the truth with complete freedom, according to our duty. Not because We forget the special circumstances of our times, nor because we judge the useful and honest advances of our time to be condemnable, but because We would like public life to run along safer paths and have more solid foundations, and this while keeping intact the true freedom of the people; this human freedom whose mother and best guarantee is the truth: "the truth will set you free"[29].

21. If, therefore, in these difficult circumstances, Catholics listen, as is their obligation, to these our teachings, they will easily understand what the duties of each one are, both in the theoretical order and in the practical order. In the order of ideas, a firm adherence to all the present and future teachings of the Roman Pontiffs and the public profession of these teachings as often as circumstances require is necessary. And in particular regarding the so-called modern freedoms, it is necessary that everyone abide by the judgment of the Apostolic See and identify with its feelings. We must guard against the danger that the honest appearance of these freedoms may deceive some unwary person. Think about the origin of these freedoms and the intentions of those who defend them. Experience has sufficiently demonstrated the results they produce in society. Everywhere they have borne fruit so pernicious that they have rightly provoked disappointment and repentance in all honest and prudent men. If we compare this kind of modern State, of which we speak, with another State, real or imaginary, that tyrannically and openly persecutes the Christian religion, the first may seem more tolerable than the second. However, the principles on which it is based are such, as we have said, that they cannot be accepted by anyone.

22. In practice, the application of these principles can be considered both in private and domestic life and in public life. In the private order, the main duty of each person is to perfectly adjust their life and conduct to the evangelical precepts, without retreating from the sacrifices and difficulties that Christian virtue imposes. Furthermore, everyone must love the Church as a common Mother; obey its laws, seek its honor, defend its rights and strive to ensure that it is respected and loved by those over whom each has some authority. It is also of public interest that Catholics correctly collaborate in municipal administration, ensuring and achieving above all that attention is paid to the public education of youth in relation to religion and good morals, as is appropriate for Christian people: the public good of each city depends greatly on this teaching. Likewise, as a general rule, it is good and useful for the action of Catholics to extend from this narrow circle to a broader field, and even to encompass the supreme power of the State. We say as a general rule because these teachings of ours are addressed to all nations. It may very well happen that somewhere, for very serious and very just reasons, it is not advisable in any way to intervene in the government of a State or to occupy political positions in it. But in general, as we have said, not wanting to take any part in public life would be as reprehensible as not wanting to give any help to the common good. All the more so since Catholics, by virtue of the very doctrine they profess, are obliged in conscience to fulfill these obligations with complete fidelity. Otherwise, if they abstain politically, political affairs will fall into the hands of people whose way of thinking can offer little hope of salvation for the State. A situation that would also result in no small damage to the Christian religion. Then the enemies of the Church could do a lot and its friends could do very little. It is, therefore, very clear that Catholics have just reasons to intervene in the political life of people. They do not and should not come to political life to approve what may currently be reprehensible in the political institutions of the State, but to ensure that these same institutions put themselves, as far as possible, at the sincere and true service of the public good, seeking to infuse all the veins of the State, like sap and vigorous blood, with the effective influence of the Catholic religion.

23. It is necessary to renew the examples of our elders in our times. It is necessary, first of all, that Catholics worthy of this name be willing to be loving children of the Church and appear as such. They must reject without hesitation everything that is incompatible with their Christian profession. They must use, to the extent that their conscience allows, public institutions to defend truth and justice. They must strive so that freedom in acting does not exceed the limits indicated by nature and by the law of God. They must ensure that all States reflect the Christian conception, which we have explained, of public life. It is not possible to point out unique and uniform guidelines in these matters, because they must be adapted to circumstances of time and place that are very different from each other. However, we must preserve, above all, the concord of wills and tend towards unity in action and purposes. This double result will be obtained without difficulty if each one takes as his standard of conduct the prescriptions of the Apostolic See and obedience to the bishops, whom the Holy Spirit appointed to govern the Church of God[31]. The defense of the Catholic religion necessarily requires unity of thought and the firm perseverance of all in the public profession of the doctrines taught by the Church. And at this point two dangers must be avoided: collusion with false opinions and a resistance less energetic than that required by the truth. However, in matters of opinion, any moderate discussion with the desire to reach the truth is lawful, but always leaving aside all unfair suspicion and all mutual accusations. Therefore, so that the union of spirits is not destroyed with reckless accusations, everyone must understand that the integrity of Catholic truth cannot in any way be combined with the opinions touched by naturalism or rationalism, whose ultimate goal is to raze the Christian religion to its foundations and establish in society the authority of man independent of God.

24. These are, venerable brothers, the teachings that We deem appropriate to give to all the nations of the Catholic world regarding the Christian constitution of the State and the obligations of the citizen.
